newsitem.title: UK: Scientists home in on brain's fear centre.
newsitem.headline: Scientists home in on brain's fear centre.

text.p: British scientists said on Wednesday they had found definitive proof that a "fear centre" in the brain helps people recognise frightened expressions on other people's faces.
Their findings add to evidence that emotional responses are "hard-wired" into the human brain and are not learned.

Ray Dolan and colleagues at the Wellcome Department of Cognitive Neurology at University College London used advanced brain scanning techniques to see which parts of a person's brain was activated when looking at people who looked scared.
They found it was a centre in the amygdala, a structure buried in the brain's temporal lobe.

The amygdala has long been linked with fear, but only through indirect studies. People with damaged amygdalas do not react to frightened faces or to things that should scare them and monkeys with their amygdalas removed are uncommonly tame.

"Our understanding of the brain is still in the early stages but clearly the brain is responsible for our whole experience of the world and everything we do. It is our emotional experience," said Dr John Morris, a psychiatrist who worked on the study.

"It seems fairly obvious that we don't really have to learn how to be emotional. It seems to be something that we are born with. There is evidence that our facial expressions are somehow hard-wired and innate, they are universal throughout cultures."
Morris' and Dolan's group used positron emission tomography (PET) to scan the brains of five volunteers who were showed pictures of faces with either happy or fearful expressions.
PET scans measure blood flow and can indicate what part of the brain is being activated.

"The faces depicted either happy or fearful expressions, and for each emotional category and individual face a range of six levels of intensity was produced by computer graphical manipulation," they wrote in the science journal Nature.
The scans showed a very specific part of the amygdala was activated when the volunteers looked at frightened faces. The more frightened the face looked, the stronger the response.
"Our results provide direct evidence that the human amygdala is involved in a neural response to fearful facial expressions," they concluded.
